items.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
items.content: At a glance Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error.  In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens.   Where the tokens go We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s…

items.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
items.content: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs…

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.content: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It inclu…

items.title: Notion’s Founder on the One Thing Your AI Is Missing
items.content: Everybody can start making their own software, no? In some sense, the original vision of the 60s, 70s, hippie generation of computing come to life, and that's actually why Notion was started. Notion was about how do we bring this computing power to as many people as possible without forcing them to learn how to code. Hello and welcome to the Every Podcast. I'm Dan Shipper. And I'm Natalia Quintero. And this week we're talking about a conversation that you had, Dan, with Ivan Zhao, CEO and founder of Notion. Can you tell me a little bit about what you learned? Yeah, it was such an interesting conversation because Notion is the original, one of the original no code companies. The way it's structured with databases and forms and blocks, it's all designed to allow you to build something that looks kind of like software without knowing how to code. But AI like totally changed that. Now anyone can Vibe code whatever they want. You don't really need a block system. You don't really need the whole Notion interface in order to make something that looks like software. And so it kind of forced them to reinvent what they are and reinvent or rethink the original vision for their product. I've been a user of Notion for a long time, and the product has evolved quite a bit. What do you think makes Ivan the right leader to lead this transformation? You know him well. Ivan is one of those interesting people. I think there's some kind of soul overlap between Notion and Every, and I think that comes from who Ivan is as a person. You know, the way that he dresses and the way that they furnish their office, and there's so much attention to detail and so much craft in what they do. And I think that that's actually sorely missing from the... pantheon of AI CEOs. Like when you really think about what kinds of CEOs are around in this era, there are very few people who care a lot about the details and the feeling of work and what you make. And especially in a world where everyone's afraid of AI taking jobs and how do you keep the work that we do feeling human or feeling special. I think that there's something really interesting happening with Notion and Ivan is the right person to make that happen. So if you didn't catch it at thesis, let's turn over now to a conversation between Dan Shipper and Ivan Zao from Notion. Welcome, really excited to have you here. Good to be here. And thank you for sponsoring this, for making this event possible. I didn't know until I got here. Yeah, Ivan asked me backstage, he was like, how much was this? And I was like, I don't know, but next time, we'll make it bigger if you want to pay a little more. It's big enough. Good love. Great. Nice to be here. So in addition to sponsoring this conference, you make Notion. And I think of you as, we were talking about this a little bit backstage. I think there is a spiritual similarity between the way that Notion and every think about work. And I think that comes from you specifically. you think a lot about the craft of work and thinking well with software. And I think when we are, like in AI there seems like there's this bifurcation between people who think it's all slop and people who think that you can actually do good work with it. And I'm curious like how you're thinking about this as you're bringing Notion into this era and in your own life. We're probably in the one year after the Vibe coding phase at this point, for most people. Probably in this room. A year ago, people say software is dead, Vibe code everything. Then nine months ago, people realized you need to maintain them. I'm actually in different directions. I love the spirit of Vibe coding. Actually, if anything, Vibe coding, the spirit is the spirit that YNOTION was started in the first place. I think so, right? Yeah. If I share this with you all, it's... When I was in school, last year college, I was inspired by early days of computing. People in the 60s and 70s, or even the 50s, their idea of a software, it's a me…

items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.content: Happy to bring to you our episode with Black Forest Labs. Our guests today are Andreas Blattmann, he also goes by Andi, who is co-inventor of latent diffusion, the technique that eventually got scaled up by Stable Diffusion and Stability AI, and they eventually split with a bunch of, uh, the core Stability AI image gen folks to form Black Forest Labs. And Dustin Podell, who I also met with Anj, uh, at one of the stories that we tell, and, uh, who worked his way up from just being a regular engineer, a freelance, like, web developer person, into a model and research lead at Stability AI, and now, uh, Black Forest Labs, creator of SDXL, Control LoRA, post-training lead on SD3, Flux Ultra, Flux.1, and Flux Context. And we go into all of these details. Um, as you may know, sometimes we're very honored to have an extended history with some of our guests, and this is one of them. You might have heard in our Anj Mittal episode where we talked about introducing each other at one of the NeurIPS's [smacks lips] and meeting Black Forest Labs for the first time. And, uh, this was right after Stable Diffusion. But what you may not have heard, and we only tell this story in this episode, is how latent space itself was started because of Stable Diffusion, directly, uh, crediting the launch for me basically quitting my job to go all in on AI based on what we saw. And today's guest, Dustin, also [chuckles] had that experience, and so did Vibhu. And so we have a very, very strong tie with the team that basically led up to Black Forest Labs, and now we're also interested in what's next for them. Like, they have created some of the best open and closed weights models for image generation and video generation. I think especially Flux Context, if you're not aware of image editing models, I do think that this is in the ex-in the limit one of the things to fully replace Canva and, um, and Photoshop and a bunch of other workflows and editors that you might use in a normal creative workflow. It is not going to replace the top end of the market. But for regular, normal, everyday edits, why would you not want anything else other than to query a model and ask it to do, uh, image editing for you? Uh, we do this obviously with this kind of video editing. It's all Clanker done, and I do review it, and they're also moving into robotics. And so this ties in with a miniseries of model labs that have been pursuing this direction, building world models from image gen, like with Runway, uh, as well as, um, video models and now robotics models. And so I think a lot of things rhyme in a lot of our recent episodes, like even the artificial analysis episode that we're gonna release soon, they are also going into robotics, and, like, it seems pretty s- obvious that when you see a whole bunch of smart people who are at the frontier all leaning one direction, that you're probably six to 12 months out from some kind of really big breakthrough. This has been a consistent theme over my last four years of podcasting. It's not gonna change now. So look out for it. Um, that's the [chuckles] most obvious call-out I can make. But there's also a lot of interesting lore for people interested in the general diffusion space. Uh, we're gonna d- do a little bit more over time. I, I'm thinking about an AI- AIE LA, where we talk about the generative media field and the creative arts and how, uh, that complicated relationship is evolving, um, and I think maturing, to be honest. And finally, for those longtime listeners, uh, we are starting to open up to advertisers, people that we really admire and respect and wanna showcase what they're working on. Um, the first one was with Supabase, which I think a lot of you enjoyed, and the second one today is brought to you by Deepgram, and you'll hear more from us at the midpoint of the episode. [upbeat music] You should be showing a robot an action one time, and then it should be able to do this, and this would be truly a superhuman intelligence…

items.title: Piggybacking to the Frontier
items.content: American data companies like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars worth of data to Chinese AI labs. A chunk of that data comes in the form of reinforcement learning (RL) environments, which labs use to post-train their models to make them excel at specific domains like coding, cyber, finance, law, and bio. Post-training, and especially RL, is one of the most important indicators of the final performance of a model. Whenever a new model within a single generation drops, the advances from the previous release are entirely due to post-training. The difference between Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, or from GPT 5.5 to GPT 5.6, is not due to a new pre-training run. Since they have the same base model, the capability gains come from researchers teaching the model to get better at specific domains. The phenomenon of American companies arming Chinese labs with the data that enables this RL should set off alarms for policymakers and those invested in the U.S.-China AI race: American companies are helping Chinese labs develop better models, and we were able to find at least nine who do so. But the business relationships between data vendors and Chinese labs are more complicated than that single hawkish line, and today, we’re diving into what’s going on. We’ll cover: What it means to sell an RL environment and how it differs from distillation The current ecosystem of China-tied data vendors To what extent American companies are selling RL environments to China Whether this is a problem that needs fixing What RL Does and Doesn’t Look Like Example RL Flows RL environments are essentially simulated worlds in which a model can train to improve its performance at specific tasks or environments. As an example, a model developer may want their model to get better at creating PowerPoint slides with pleasant aesthetics and clear text. To achieve that capability, the model developer may go to a data vendor and ask them to make…

items.title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
items.content: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models. Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails. At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat. We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then e…

items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.content: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting bille…
items.summary: ArtCraft used AI to rewrite Photoshop as open source software. For CEO Brandon Thomas, the vision is even bigger: to take back the internet!

items.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
items.content: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate ev…

items.title: Why the Cyberpocalypse Might Hit China Harder
items.content: Chang Che is a writer and contributor to the New Yorker . In August, researchers at a California security firm used an OpenAI model to find a software bug in PHP, a programming language that undergird some seventy per cent of the world’s websites, including Wikipedia and WordPress. They alerted PHP’s developers, who quietly began working on a fix. By late October, the fix was ready, but before they could alert the world, the break-in attempts had begun. Days earlier, Amazon detected someone trying to hack into its servers; attacks code began circulating online. Some governments and companies began pulling websites down, rather than risk a security breach. One security firm described the flaws as some of the worst ever found in PHP, “and arguably in software history.” Before AI, the internet might have looked, to a hacker, like a worn-out bug screen. You could discern some holes with a keen eye, and that knowledge was reliably asymmetric—others probably didn’t know about the holes you found. Moreover, tunneling through the holes undetected took months or years of human labor, talent, and money. Now, with AI, the internet looks more like a block of Swiss cheese: the holes are obvious, anyone can, or will, see them, and the time and cost it takes to exploit these software flaws have plunged alarmingly fast . According to Google’s incident response team , the average time it takes for cyber criminals to exploit a new vulnerability is -7 days, meaning hacking attempts are “routinely occurring before a patch is even released.” A China Central Television (CCTV) feature about the PHP vulnerability discovered by cybersecurity firm Calif, with the aid of OpenAI models. Source . Hackers refer to unbeknownst software bugs like PHP as “zero-days” because a defender has had zero days to protect themselves upon its discovery. Once a hacker discovers a zero-day in, say, iOS software, every iPhone user is potentially…
